niddah-6a-11-12.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once decided a real case following the view of Rabbi Eliezer: a woman who has gone three expected cycles without bleeding is not made impure retroactively when she bleeds again. Afterward he remembered that other Sages disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer, and he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances. The Gemara then asks what it was that he remembered.
niddah-6a-11-12.why: The Gemara is testing Rav Huna's view that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity does not affect teruma. This case, which must have involved teruma, implies the majority view makes teruma impure retroactively, contradicting Rav Huna.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; ruled in this case according to Rabbi Eliezer and then reconsidered.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi followed; other Sages disagreed with him.

terms.meaning: A situation of pressing need, when a minority opinion may be relied on even though the law normally follows the majority.
The rule that a woman who finds menstrual blood may be treated as having been ritually impure for a period before she noticed it, affecting pure foods she touched in that time.

niddah-6b-4-4.note: Rabban Gamliel's maidservant was baking loaves of teruma, and between each loaf she washed her hand and examined herself. After the last one she found she was impure from menstrual blood, and she asked Rabban Gamliel. He told her all the loaves were impure. She said: My teacher, did I not examine myself between each one? He answered: If so, this last one is impure and all the rest are pure.
niddah-6b-4-4.why: Rav Huna holds that a menstruating woman's retroactive impurity reaches sacrificial food but not teruma. Since Rabban Gamliel applied it to teruma loaves, the Gemara cites this as a challenge, then answers that these were loaves of a thanks offering.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules on the status of the loaves his maidservant baked.

terms.meaning: The portion of produce given to priests, which must be kept ritually pure.
A woman checks for menstrual blood, since finding it makes her ritually impure and can make what she touched impure as well.

niddah-6b-8-8.note: Another time, Rabban Gamliel's maidservant was sealing barrels of wine, washing her hands and examining herself between each one. After the last one she found she was impure, and she asked Rabban Gamliel, who said all the barrels were impure. She reminded him that she had examined herself between each one, and he ruled: If so, this last one is impure and all the rest are pure.
niddah-6b-8-8.why: The Gemara is testing Rav Huna's view that retroactive menstrual impurity applies to sacrificial food but not teruma. If both incidents involved sacrificial food, why would she ask twice? The Gemara answers that they happened to two different maidservants.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rules on the status of the wine barrels his maidservant sealed.

terms.meaning: A woman checks for menstrual blood, since finding it makes her ritually impure and can make what she touched impure as well.

niddah-9b-7-8.note: Rabbi Eliezer recalls a girl in the village of Hitlo who stopped menstruating for three cycles and then bled again. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that 'her time is sufficient': she is impure only from the moment she saw blood, not retroactively. The other Sages answered Rabbi Eliezer that a ruling made in exigent circumstances is no proof. The Gemara gives two accounts of the emergency: some say it was during years of famine, others that the girl had handled many ritually pure items and the Sages did not want them all lost.
niddah-9b-7-8.why: The mishna records Rabbi Eliezer's view that any woman who goes three cycles without bleeding is impure only from the time she sees blood; this incident is his proof. The Gemara next tells how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi relied on Rabbi Eliezer in exactly such an emergency.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage who cites the incident as proof for his ruling, against the other Sages.

terms.meaning: A woman whose status this describes becomes impure only from the moment she sees blood. Otherwise, a woman can be treated as impure retroactively, so that pure items she touched in the preceding hours become impure.
An emergency or time of great need, when the Sages might rule leniently. The other Sages argue that such a ruling cannot serve as a precedent for ordinary times.
Food and objects kept in a state of ritual purity, which become unusable for that purpose if touched by someone impure.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-9b-9-9.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi once ruled in a case according to the opinion of Rabbi Eliezer. After he remembered, he said: Rabbi Eliezer is worthy to rely upon in exigent circumstances. The Gemara then asks what 'after he remembered' means: if he remembered that the law had been decided against Rabbi Eliezer, how could he follow him even in an emergency?
niddah-9b-9-9.why: The Sages had just dismissed Rabbi Eliezer's precedent as an emergency ruling. The Gemara answers its question by explaining that no ruling had yet been fixed; Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi remembered that many Sages, not one, disagreed with Rabbi Eliezer.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply 'Rabbi'; he ruled as Rabbi Eliezer did and then defended relying on him in an emergency.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The Sage whose lenient view about a woman who missed three cycles Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi followed.

terms.meaning: An emergency or time of great need, when a lenient minority opinion might be relied upon.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-13a-19-19.note: Rav Yehuda and his teacher Shmuel were standing on the roof of the synagogue in Neharde'a. Rav Yehuda said to Shmuel that he needed to urinate. Shmuel told him: Shinnana, hold your penis and urinate outward, so that the water would fall away from the synagogue roof rather than onto it.
niddah-13a-19-19.why: The Gemara has been warning that a man should not hold his penis, lest he emit semen for naught. It asks how Rav Yehuda could do so, and Abaye answers that fear kept him from sexual thoughts, as frightened marauders are presumed not to pour wine for idols.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: Shmuel's student, who needed to urinate while on the synagogue roof.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Rav Yehuda's teacher, who told him how to urinate without wetting the synagogue roof.

terms.meaning: A nickname Shmuel used for Rav Yehuda, usually understood as 'sharp one'.

niddah-14b-3-6.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi kept praising Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa to Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, as a great man, and Rabbi Yishmael asked to meet him. When Rabbi Ḥama came, Rabbi Yishmael invited him to ask a question. Rabbi Ḥama asked about a woman who examined herself with a cloth she had not checked beforehand, put it in a box, and found blood on it the next day. Rabbi Yishmael offered to answer by his father Rabbi Yosei's view or by Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's; Rabbi Ḥama chose Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's. Rabbi Yishmael scoffed: is this the great man? How can he set aside the teacher's words and listen to the student's?
niddah-14b-3-6.why: The Gemara has just discussed this very case of blood found on an unchecked cloth in a box. After the story it explains Rabbi Ḥama's choice and identifies the two views: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi deems the woman impure and Rabbi Yosei deems her pure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called 'Rabbi'; he praised Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa. He had been a student of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥama bar Bisa
people.about: The scholar praised as a great man, who asked the question and chose Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi's ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Asked to meet Rabbi Ḥama, then mocked his choice of the student's view over his father's.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: Rabbi Yishmael's father, called the teacher of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi.

terms.meaning: A cloth a woman uses to check herself for menstrual blood. Here it had not been checked for stains before use, so it is unclear where the blood came from.
Jewish law, or the binding ruling on a particular question.

niddah-15b-10-11.note: In the town of Rimon, the slave woman of an olive harvester threw a stillborn baby into a pit. A priest came and looked into the pit to see whether it was a boy or a girl. The case came before the Sages, who ruled that the priest had not become impure, because martens and hyenas were common there and had probably already dragged the body away.
niddah-15b-10-11.why: The Gemara is testing the rule that a doubt cannot override something certain. Here the baby was certainly thrown in and only doubtfully removed, yet the Sages ruled leniently; the Gemara answers that it was only doubtful the object was a baby at all.

terms.meaning: A kohen, a descendant of Aaron. Priests must avoid impurity from the dead, including being under the same roof as a corpse or leaning over one.
Not carrying the ritual impurity that, in Jewish law, comes from contact with a corpse and bars a person from holy food and places.
A teaching from the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-20a-2-2.note: Ameimar, Mar Zutra and Rav Ashi were sitting before a bloodletter for treatment. The bloodletter drew blood from Ameimar into a first horn; Ameimar looked at it and told his colleagues that this is the red that the mishna speaks of. The bloodletter drew more blood into another horn, and Ameimar said its color had changed. Rav Ashi said that a Sage like himself, who cannot tell the one from the other, should not examine blood at all.
niddah-20a-2-2.why: The mishna lists the shades of blood that make a woman impure, and Rav Naḥman has said that its red is like the blood of bloodletting. This scene puts that comparison to the eye and shows how fine the distinctions are.

people.name: Ameimar
people.about: The Sage whose blood was drawn and who identified the mishna's red in it.

people.name: Mar Zutra
people.about: A colleague sitting with Ameimar and Rav Ashi before the bloodletter.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Could not see the difference between the two samples and concluded he should not judge blood.

terms.meaning: A horn used by a bloodletter to draw and collect blood, a common medical treatment at the time.
Examining a woman's blood stain to rule whether its color makes her ritually impure or leaves her pure.
The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments.

niddah-20a-6-6.note: Ulla held that the black blood the mishna calls impure is like the very black garments worn in Siva'a. When Ulla came to Pumbedita, he saw an Arab dressed in a black garment and told the Sages there that this is the black of the mishna. People tore the garment off the man bit by bit, each wanting a sample of the shade, and paid him four hundred dinars for it.
niddah-20a-6-6.why: The mishna says blood as black as ink is impure, and the Sages are trying to pin down exactly which black it means; Ulla's comparison is one of several, followed by Rabbi Yoḥanan's comparison to the cloths of bath attendants.

people.name: Ulla
people.about: The Sage who visited Pumbedita and pointed to the Arab's garment as the mishna's black.

terms.meaning: The earliest written collection of Jewish law, on which the Gemara comments. Here it lists the colors of blood that make a woman impure.

niddah-20b-5-5.note: A woman brought blood to Rabbi Elazar for examination while Rabbi Ami was sitting before him. Rabbi Elazar smelled it and told her it was blood of desire, not menstrual blood. After she left, Rabbi Ami caught up with her and asked about her situation. She told him her husband had been away on a journey and she had desired him. Rabbi Ami applied to Rabbi Elazar the verse 'The counsel of the Lord is with those who fear Him.'
niddah-20b-5-5.why: Ulla had just refused to examine blood in Pumbedita, citing Rabbi Elazar, 'the master of the Land of Israel', who would not examine blood away from home. The Gemara asks why he had that title, and this story is the answer.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: Called the master of the Land of Israel; he identified the blood by its smell.

people.name: Rabbi Ami
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's student, who checked with the woman and confirmed his teacher's ruling.

terms.meaning: Bleeding caused by a woman's longing for her husband rather than by menstruation, and so not making her impure.

niddah-20b-6-7.note: Ifera Hurmiz, mother of King Shapur, was keeping the laws of menstruation and sent blood to Rava to examine. With Rav Ovadya sitting before him, Rava smelled it and told her it was blood of desire. She told her son to see how wise the Jews are; he answered that it may have been a lucky guess. So she sent Rava sixty kinds of blood, and he identified every one except the last, which was lice blood. Without knowing it, he sent her a gift of a comb for killing lice. She exclaimed that the Jews must dwell in the chambers of people's hearts.
niddah-20b-6-7.why: It follows the account of Rabbi Elazar identifying blood of desire by its smell, in a run of stories about the Sages' skill, and caution, in examining blood.

people.name: Ifera Hurmiz
people.about: Mother of King Shapur; she sent blood to Rava and then tested him with sixty samples.

people.name: King Shapur
people.about: Ifera Hurmiz's son, who suggested Rava's first answer was a lucky guess.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who examined her blood and identified nearly all the samples.

people.name: Rav Ovadya
people.about: Was sitting before Rava when he examined the blood.

terms.meaning: Bleeding caused by a woman's longing for her husband rather than by menstruation, and so not making her impure.

terms.term: A blind man through a chimney
terms.meaning: A proverb for a lucky hit: a blind man who happens to escape through the one opening.

niddah-20b-10-12.note: Yalta, Rav Naḥman's wife, brought blood to Rabba bar bar Ḥana, who deemed her impure. She then brought it to Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda, who deemed her pure. The Gemara asks how he could, since a baraita teaches that once one authority has declared something impure another may not declare it pure. It explains that at first he too deemed her impure, but she told him that Rabba bar bar Ḥana deems blood of this color pure every day, and ruled otherwise only now because his eye hurt. Then he deemed her pure.
niddah-20b-10-12.why: The Gemara goes on to ask whether a woman is believed when she makes claims like Yalta's about her blood, and later returns to this case as a possible proof.

people.name: Yalta
people.about: Rav Naḥman's wife, who took her blood to a second Sage after the first deemed it impure.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Ḥana
people.about: The Sage who deemed her impure; Yalta said his eye was hurting that day.

people.name: Rav Yitzḥak, son of Rav Yehuda
people.about: The second Sage, who deemed her pure after hearing her explanation.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.
Ruled whether the blood's color makes the woman ritually impure as a menstruating woman, which forbids marital relations until she immerses.

niddah-20b-19-20.note: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi examined a woman's blood at night and declared it impure. Looking at it again by day, he declared it pure. He waited an hour and declared it impure again. Then he said: Woe is me! Perhaps I erred.
niddah-20b-19-20.why: The Gemara is discussing how Sages examined blood and whether one may rule on it based on how it would have looked earlier; it questions his worry, citing a rule that one may not say the blood would have been impure had it been moist, and then rereads the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi
people.about: Called simply Rabbi; examined the blood three times, changed his ruling twice and feared he had erred.

terms.meaning: A woman who found a stain could bring it to a Sage, who judged by its color whether it was menstrual blood making her ritually impure, or a color that leaves her pure.
Ritual status, not hygiene. A woman who is impure from menstruation may not have relations with her husband or touch certain sacred foods until she purifies herself.

niddah-22b-2-3.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Tzadok, tells of two cases his father brought from Tivin to the Sages in Yavne. A woman kept discharging things like red shells; people asked his father, his father asked the Sages, and the Sages asked the doctors, who said she had a wound in her womb. The ruling was that she should put them in water, and if they dissolved she is impure. In a second case a woman discharged things like red hairs; the doctors said she had a mole in her womb, and the same water test was given.
niddah-22b-2-3.why: The mishna says a woman who discharges red items like shells or hairs should put them in water to see if they are blood. When the Gemara asks whether such cases ever really happen, these two incidents show that they do.

terms.meaning: Here, the ritual impurity of a menstruating woman: if the items dissolve, they are blood, and she has that status.

niddah-24a-9-10.note: The sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya went out to the villages, and when they came back their father asked whether any case had come to them for a ruling. They told him that a woman had miscarried a fetus with a flat face and they had deemed her impure as a woman after childbirth. Rabbi Ḥiyya told them to go out and declare pure what they had declared impure. If they thought they were being strict, he said, it was a stringency that leads to a leniency, because they had also given her the days of purity that follow childbirth.
niddah-24a-9-10.why: Rabbi Yoḥanan and Reish Lakish disagree about a woman who miscarries a fetus whose face is flat; Rabbi Ḥiyya's ruling to his sons treats such a fetus as not a birth at all.

people.name: Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Father of the sons; he reversed their ruling.

people.name: Sons of Rabbi Ḥiyya
people.about: Ruled on the case while away in the villages and were told to undo their ruling.

terms.term: Impurity of a woman after childbirth
terms.meaning: After giving birth a woman is impure for a set period, seven days for a boy and fourteen for a girl, by the Torah's rules.
The weeks after that period of impurity during which, by the Torah's rules, bleeding does not make a woman who has given birth impure.

terms.term: A stringency that leads to a leniency
terms.meaning: A strict ruling that ends up producing a lenient result, here by treating bleeding in the coming weeks as pure.

niddah-24b-10-11.note: A woman discharged something shaped like a snake, and Ḥanina, Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew, ruled her impure as a woman after childbirth. Rabbi Yosef told Rabban Gamliel, who sent word to Rabbi Yehoshua to bring his nephew to him. On the way, Ḥanina's daughter-in-law came out and asked Rabbi Yehoshua about such a case. He said the mother is pure. She replied that her mother-in-law had told her in his name that the mother is impure, because a snake's eye is round like a human's. Her words reminded him, and he sent to Rabban Gamliel: Ḥanina ruled on my authority.
niddah-24b-10-11.why: The Gemara has just ruled that a fetus shaped like a lilith counts as a birth. From this story Abaye learns that a scholar should state the reason for his ruling, so that when reminded of it he will remember the ruling.

people.name: Ḥanina
people.about: Rabbi Yehoshua's nephew, who ruled the woman impure.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Ḥanina's uncle; he had forgotten his own ruling until reminded.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Summoned Rabbi Yehoshua and his nephew over the ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Yosef
people.about: Reported Ḥanina's ruling to Rabban Gamliel.

terms.term: Impure as a woman after childbirth
terms.meaning: Treating the discharge as a real birth, so the mother has the Torah's period of impurity that follows childbirth.

niddah-24b-17-17.note: Abba Shaul, or some say Rabbi Yoḥanan, recalls his days as a gravedigger. Once he chased a deer and ran into the thighbone of a corpse. He ran after the deer for three parasangs inside it, never caught the deer, and never reached the end of the bone. When he came back, he was told it was the thighbone of Og, king of Bashan.
niddah-24b-17-17.why: Abaye has spoken of undiluted wine harming an embryo, and the Gemara cited Abba Shaul's gravedigger observations on wine and bones; this is another of his gravedigging reports, followed by a third.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A gravedigger who tells this story about himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: Some say the story is his rather than Abba Shaul's.

people.name: Og, king of Bashan
people.about: A giant king from the Bible; the bone was said to be his.

terms.meaning: A Persian measure of distance, roughly a few miles.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-24b-18-18.note: Abba Shaul recalls his days as a gravedigger. Once a burial cave opened beneath him, and he found himself standing in the eye socket of a corpse, sunk up to his nose. When he came back, he was told it was the eye of Absalom.
niddah-24b-18-18.why: It is the third of Abba Shaul's gravedigger reports. The Gemara then insists he was no midget but the tallest man of his generation, and lists each generation's tallest man, each reaching only the shoulder of the one before.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: A gravedigger who tells this story about himself.

people.name: Absalom
people.about: King David's son in the Bible; the eye was said to be his.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-25b-8-9.note: A gestational sac a woman had discharged was brought before Mar Shmuel. He said the embryo was forty-one days old. He then counted from the day she had gone to immerse in the ritual bath and found only forty days. He told the court that her husband had had intercourse with her while she was a menstruating woman. They bound the husband, and he confessed.
niddah-25b-8-9.why: Shmuel had ruled that a woman who discharges such a sac must be concerned it was a birth, as if he were unsure. The Gemara asks how he could be unsure given this story, and answers that Shmuel was exceptional; his cautious rule is for others less skilled.

people.name: Mar Shmuel
people.about: Shmuel; he dated the embryo exactly and so exposed the husband.

terms.meaning: The membrane that surrounds an early embryo, here discharged in a miscarriage.
A woman immerses in a ritual bath at the end of her menstrual impurity, after which she and her husband may resume relations.
A woman in her period of menstrual impurity, with whom intercourse is forbidden until she immerses.

niddah-26b-9-10.note: Shmuel, Rav's students and Rav Yehuda were sitting together when Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of D'vil, came hurrying toward them. Shmuel remarked that here came a man one could knock down with a straw of wheat, and he would fall and stay down. When Rav Yosef arrived, Shmuel asked him what Rav had said about an afterbirth. He answered that Rav said an afterbirth is attributed only to a viable offspring. Shmuel asked all of Rav's students, and they confirmed it. Then Shmuel looked harshly at Rav Yehuda, a student of Rav who had not passed this teaching on to him.
niddah-26b-9-10.why: The discussion has been about whether an afterbirth discharged after a birth is linked to that birth, and about conflicting reports of what Rav said; this story records Rav's ruling as his students confirmed it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: Asked what Rav had said and was annoyed that Rav Yehuda had not told him.

people.name: Rav Yosef, son of Rav Menashya of D'vil
people.about: The man Shmuel belittled, who then reported Rav's ruling correctly.

people.name: Rav Yehuda
people.about: A student of Rav who had not passed this ruling on to Shmuel.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling on the afterbirth is in question.

terms.meaning: The placenta and membranes expelled after a birth. The question is whether a separate afterbirth means a second, unseen offspring was miscarried.
A baby that can survive, as opposed to a non-viable newborn.

niddah-30b-5-5.note: The Rabbis told Rabbi Yishmael of Cleopatra, Queen of Alexandria. Her maidservants had been sentenced to death by the government, and she experimented on them to see how long an embryo takes to form; she found that both male and female embryos were formed by the forty-first day. Rabbi Yishmael answered: I bring you proof from the Torah, and you bring me proof from the fools?
niddah-30b-5-5.why: Rabbi Yishmael holds that a male embryo forms in forty-one days and a female in eighty-one, deriving it from the Torah's periods of impurity after birth. The Rabbis cite Cleopatra against him; the Gemara then explains why he called her proof one from fools.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Held that a female embryo takes twice as long to form as a male, and rejected the Rabbis' proof.

people.name: Cleopatra
people.about: Queen of Alexandria, who experimented on her condemned maidservants.

terms.meaning: The point at which an embryo has taken recognizable shape, which affects whether a woman who miscarries counts as having given birth.

niddah-30b-10-10.note: In this telling, Rabbi Yishmael is the one who cites Cleopatra, the Greek queen. Her maidservants had been sentenced to death by the government; she experimented on them and found that a male embryo was formed on the forty-first day and a female on the eighty-first. The Rabbis answered him: One does not bring proof from the fools.
niddah-30b-10-10.why: The Gemara has just discussed a version in which the Rabbis cited Cleopatra against Rabbi Yishmael; this second baraita reverses the roles, and the Gemara goes on to explain why the Rabbis dismissed the proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Cites Cleopatra's findings as support for his view.

people.name: Cleopatra
people.about: Called the Greek queen; she experimented on her condemned maidservants.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the core collection of Jewish law.

niddah-31a-15-15.note: Two people set out on a business trip. A thorn pierced one of them, so he could not go, and he began blaspheming and cursing. Some time later he heard that his companion's ship had sunk at sea, and he began thanking and praising God. That, the teaching concludes, is why the verse says 'Your anger is turned away, and You comfort me.'
niddah-31a-15-15.why: Rav Yosef asks what Isaiah means by 'I will give thanks to You, Lord, for You were angry with me'; this case is his answer. Rabbi Elazar's teaching follows, that even the one a miracle is done for does not recognize it.

niddah-33b-5-10.note: Rav Pappa came to the town of Tavakh and said he would greet any Torah scholar there. An old woman told him of Rav Shmuel, who teaches mishnayot, and blessed Rav Pappa that he should be like him; Rav Pappa concluded that Rav Shmuel must be God-fearing. Rav Shmuel slaughtered a bull in his honor and challenged him with two teachings that seem to contradict each other on burning teruma over a doubtful impurity. Rav Pappa prayed that the bull be eaten in peace and gave an answer, but Rav Shmuel knocked it down. Rav Pappa left and went to Rav Shimi bar Ashi, who asked him why he had not answered with a better case: a Samaritan who had immersed and then trod on the garments of a careful observer, which then touched teruma.
niddah-33b-5-10.why: The mishna has just said that teruma is not burned over garments a Samaritan lay on, because their impurity is uncertain. The visit turns on that very ruling, and the Gemara goes on to explain Rav Shimi's answer as a double doubt.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Sage who visits Tavakh and is challenged by his host.

people.name: Rav Shmuel
people.about: A Torah scholar in Tavakh who teaches mishnayot and hosts Rav Pappa.

people.name: Rav Shimi bar Ashi
people.about: The Sage Rav Pappa goes to afterward, who suggests the answer he could have given.

terms.meaning: A portion of produce given to the priests. It must be kept ritually pure; teruma that becomes impure is burned.
Plural of mishna: the short teachings of the early Sages that the Talmud discusses.
A Jew who is not careful about the rules of ritual purity, so the Sages treat his garments as likely impure.
A person known to be scrupulous about ritual purity, tithes and teruma.

niddah-33b-17-19.note: A Sadducee was talking with the High Priest in the marketplace when spit flew from his mouth onto the High Priest's garments. The High Priest's face turned green, fearing his garments were now impure, and he hurried to the Sadducee's wife to ask about her practice. She told him that although they are Sadducee wives, they fear the Pharisees and show their blood to the Sages. Rabbi Yosei adds that he knew these women better than anyone and they all did so, except for one woman in his neighborhood who did not show her blood to the Sages, and she died.
niddah-33b-17-19.why: The Gemara has just ruled that Sadducee women are by default treated like Samaritan women in menstrual purity. This baraita suggests they did consult the Sages; the Gemara then asks why the High Priest did not fear an ordinary man's spit.

people.name: High Priest
people.about: Unnamed; his garments are struck by a Sadducee's spit and he fears they are impure.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who says he knew the Sadducee wives well, as neighbors.

terms.meaning: A member of a Jewish group that rejected many of the Sages' teachings, including their rules on menstrual purity.

terms.term: show their blood to the Sages
terms.meaning: A woman unsure whether a stain was menstrual blood would show it to a Sage, who ruled whether she was impure.
The Pharisees, the party of the Sages, who were careful about ritual purity.

niddah-36b-21-24.note: Sheila bar Avina ruled in a real case following Rav. As Rav was dying, he told Rav Asi to go and tell Sheila the ruling was wrong, and if he did not listen, to drag him over with arguments; Rav Asi misheard it as 'excommunicate him'. After Rav died, Sheila refused, saying Rav would have told him himself, and Rav Asi excommunicated him. Sheila asked if he did not fear the fire; Rav Asi called himself a copper mortar that rot cannot touch, and Sheila answered that he was an iron pestle that smashes copper. Rav Asi fell ill, swinging between fever and chills, and died. Sheila asked his wife to prepare his shrouds so Rav Asi would not speak against him to Rav, and he too died. At the funeral the myrtle flew from one bier to the other, and people said the Sages had made peace.
niddah-36b-21-24.why: The Gemara has been deriving from verses that blood from labor pains during the days of ziva is pure. The story shows that Rav, who held otherwise, took back his view before he died.

people.name: Sheila bar Avina
people.about: Rav's student, who ruled following Rav and would not accept Rav's retraction from a messenger.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The teacher whose ruling Sheila followed; on his deathbed he sends word that it was wrong.

people.name: Rav Asi
people.about: The Sage Rav sends to Sheila; he mishears Rav's instruction and excommunicates Sheila.

terms.meaning: To place someone under a ban: the community keeps its distance from him until the ban is lifted.
A flow of blood outside a woman's regular menstrual period, which carries its own rules of ritual impurity.
A fragrant branch customarily laid on a bier at a funeral.

niddah-42b-5-6.note: A man asked Rava whether one may circumcise on Shabbat, and Rava said yes. After the man left, Rava wondered how anyone could not know something so basic, so he went after him and asked how the case had actually happened. The man said he had heard the baby crying at nightfall on Friday, before Shabbat, but it was not born until Shabbat. Rava told him the baby had already put its head out, so it counted as born on Friday; a circumcision done after its proper day does not override Shabbat.
niddah-42b-5-6.why: The Gemara has just cited Rav Oshaya: once a baby puts its head out of the birth canal, it counts as born. Rava's case applies that rule to work out a baby's circumcision day.

people.name: Rava
people.about: A Sage who answers a man's question and then follows him to learn what really happened.

terms.meaning: The Sages' term for the birth canal. A baby whose head has come out of it counts as born.

terms.term: circumcision not at its appointed time
terms.meaning: Circumcision is done on the eighth day after birth and overrides Shabbat only then; if it is delayed, it may not be done on Shabbat.

niddah-45a-8-9.note: Yusteni, daughter of Asveirus son of the Roman emperor Antoninus, came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi with questions. She asked at what age a woman may marry, and he said three years and one day; she asked at what age a woman can become pregnant, and he said twelve years and one day. She told him she had married at six and given birth at seven, and said: woe for the three years I wasted in my father's house.
niddah-45a-8-9.why: The mishna has just treated three years and one day as the age from which intercourse with a girl counts in law. The Gemara then asks how Yusteni could have become pregnant so young, since a baraita assumes girls under eleven cannot conceive.

people.name: Yusteni
people.about: A gentile woman, daughter of Asveirus son of the Roman emperor Antoninus, who questions Rabbi.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, the Sage who answers Yusteni's questions.

terms.meaning: A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.

niddah-45a-15-17.note: A woman came to Rabbi Akiva and told him she had had intercourse before she was three years old, and asked whether she could marry a priest. He told her she could. She then gave him a parable: a baby whose finger is dipped in honey protests the first and second time, but the third time sucks it; she meant that she had come to consent. Rabbi Akiva then told her she was unfit for the priesthood. Seeing his students look at each other, he asked what troubled them, and they said that a girl under three being fit for the priesthood is a law handed down from Moses at Sinai. The Gemara adds that Rabbi Akiva had said it only to sharpen his students.
niddah-45a-15-17.why: The Gemara has been asking whether a girl under three who has had intercourse keeps her virginal status. This baraita states as a law from Sinai that she may still marry a priest, whether or not she consented.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage the woman asks; he tests his students with a ruling he does not hold.

terms.meaning: Allowed to marry a priest. A priest may not marry a woman who has had certain kinds of forbidden intercourse.

terms.term: halakha transmitted to Moses from Sinai
terms.meaning: A law with no source in a verse, held to have been given orally to Moses at Sinai.

niddah-47a-14-14.note: Shmuel examined his maidservant for the bodily signs that mark a girl's stages of growing up, and afterward paid her four dinars for her humiliation. The Gemara explains that he was acting on his own teaching: the verse 'you may enslave them forever' means slaves were given for service, not for humiliation.
niddah-47a-14-14.why: The mishna lists the signs that a girl has reached grown womanhood, and Shmuel has just explained one of them, a fold below the breast. The Gemara tells how he checked those signs himself.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage who examines his maidservant for the signs of maturity and pays her for the humiliation.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish woman held as a slave by a Jewish master.
Damages owed by someone who shames another person.

niddah-52a-12-16.note: Rav Kahana's colleagues planned to let a young girl refuse her marriage even though she had had intercourse with her husband after showing the first signs of puberty. Rav Kahana reminded them of the case of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter. She came to the study hall to refuse her marriage with her son riding on her shoulders, and that same day her father's teaching allowing such a refusal was mentioned, and she wept greatly. The Sages said: should his own offspring stumble on what that righteous man taught? They voted and decided that a girl may refuse only until she grows two pubic hairs. The colleagues dropped their plan.
niddah-52a-12-16.why: Rabbi Elazar has ruled that the law follows Rabbi Yehuda, who lets a girl refuse for longer; but the Gemara adds that even Rabbi Yehuda agrees that intercourse after two hairs ends her right. Rav Kahana's case shows that limit being upheld.

people.name: Rav Kahana
people.about: A Sage who stops his colleagues by recalling the case of Rabbi Yishmael's daughter.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael's daughter
people.about: Married as a minor; she came to the study hall to refuse her marriage while already a mother.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael
people.about: Her father, a righteous Sage whose teaching allowed such a refusal.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.
The growth of two pubic hairs, the legal sign that a girl has reached puberty.
The house of study where the Sages met to learn and decide the law.

niddah-52a-17-17.note: Rabbi Yitzhak and the disciples of Rabbi Hanina allowed a young girl to refuse her marriage even though she had had intercourse with her husband after showing the first signs of puberty. Rav Shemen bar Abba reported it to Rabbi Yohanan, who reported it to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia. Rabbi Yehuda Nesia sent a constable and removed her from her second husband.
niddah-52a-17-17.why: Just before, Rav Kahana's colleagues dropped a plan to rule this way once they heard of the Sages' vote. Here others actually did rule this way, and the ruling was overturned by force.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage who, with Rabbi Hanina's disciples, allowed the girl to refuse.

people.name: Rav Shemen bar Abba
people.about: Reported the ruling to Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: Passed the report on to Rabbi Yehuda Nesia.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda Nesia
people.about: The leader who sent a constable to remove the girl from her second husband.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.

niddah-52b-5-6.note: Rabbi Shimon tells how Hanina ben Hakhinai met him in Tzaidan and gave him a message for Rabbi Akiva. If Akiva said a girl may refuse her marriage only until she grows two hairs, Rabbi Shimon was to remind him that ben Shelakot had testified in front of them all at Yavne that she may refuse until the area is filled with hair, and no one had objected. When Rabbi Shimon came to Rabbi Akiva, Akiva said he did not know what this 'filling' was, did not know any ben Shelakot, and held that she may refuse until she grows two hairs.
niddah-52b-5-6.why: The baraita has just listed four views on how long a girl may refuse, ending with ben Shelakot's. Rabbi Shimon's account shows Rabbi Akiva rejecting that view.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who tells the story and carries the message to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Hanina ben Hakhinai
people.about: Meets Rabbi Shimon in Tzaidan and sends a challenge to Rabbi Akiva.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Rejects the challenge and holds to the rule of two hairs.

people.name: ben Shelakot
people.about: Said to have testified at Yavne that a girl may refuse until the area is filled with hair.

terms.meaning: A girl married as a minor by her mother or brothers, after her father's death, could end the marriage simply by refusing it before she came of age.
The town where the Sages gathered as their central court and study house.

niddah-58b-5-6.note: A woman came to Rabbi Akiva and told him she had found a blood stain. He asked whether she had a wound; she said yes, but it had healed. He asked whether it could reopen and bleed; she said yes, and Rabbi Akiva declared her pure. Seeing his students look at each other, he asked what troubled them. He explained that the Sages made the rule about stains to be lenient, not strict, since the verse says 'blood' makes a woman impure, not a stain.
niddah-58b-5-6.why: The mishna has just taught that a woman may blame a stain on a wound that has scabbed over but could reopen. This incident is that ruling in practice.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: The Sage who rules on the woman's stain and explains his lenient ruling to his students.

terms.meaning: Here, not in the impure state of a menstruating woman, so she is permitted to her husband.
A spot of blood found on a woman's body or clothes. By Torah law only blood felt flowing makes her impure; impurity from stains is a rule of the Sages.

niddah-60b-7-9.note: Rav Hiyya bar Rav Mattana taught in Rav's name that the law follows Rabbi Nehemya. Rav Nahman objected that his father taught of a case where the Sages ruled women impure. The Gemara gives that teaching: two women grinding at a hand mill, and the rule for whom blood found beneath or between them makes impure. Then came the case itself: blood was found on the edge of a bathtub, and in another case on an olive leaf while women were lighting an oven, and the Sages ruled them impure.
niddah-60b-7-9.why: Rabbi Nehemya holds that a stain found on something that cannot become impure does not make a woman impure. An olive leaf is such a thing, so Rav Nahman uses this case against ruling with him; Rav Hiyya replies that the early Sages disagreed and the ruling followed Rabbi Nehemya.

people.name: Rav Hiyya bar Rav Mattana
people.about: Teaches in Rav's name that the law follows Rabbi Nehemya.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: Objects, citing a teaching from his father about a case the Sages ruled on.

terms.meaning: Here, in the impure state of a menstruating woman because of the blood found.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna but is quoted in the Talmud.

niddah-61a-10-10.note: Rabbi Meir told of a sycamore tree in Kefar Sava that people believed had a corpse buried under it. They dug and found nothing. Some days later the wind uprooted the tree, and a skull was found stuck in its roots. The Sages answered him that this proves nothing: perhaps they had not searched thoroughly enough.
niddah-61a-10-10.why: The mishna compares three women and a blood stain to a pile of stones that may hide part of a corpse, where Rabbi Meir and the Rabbis disagree on whether a search can be trusted. This is the first of several cases the Gemara cites about searches that failed.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who tells of the tree, arguing that a search for a corpse cannot be relied on.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.

niddah-61a-11-11.note: Rabbi Yosei told of a cave in Shihin that people believed held a corpse. They dug until they reached ground as smooth as a fingernail and found nothing. Some days later workers took shelter there from the rain, dug with their shovels, and found a mortar full of bones. The Sages answered him that this proves nothing: perhaps they had not searched thoroughly enough.
niddah-61a-11-11.why: The Gemara is collecting cases on whether a search for a hidden corpse can be trusted, the question behind the mishna's comparison of the three women to a pile of stones. This follows Rabbi Meir's case of the sycamore and gets the same reply.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who tells of the cave in Shihin.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.
A heavy stone bowl used for grinding.

niddah-61a-12-12.note: Abba Shaul told of a stretch of bedrock at Beit Horon that people believed held a corpse, but it was too large for the Sages to search. An old man there, Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya, asked for sheets, soaked them in water and spread them over the rock. Where the ground was pure the sheets stayed dry, and where it was impure they were moist. They dug there and found a large pit full of bones.
niddah-61a-12-12.why: The Gemara has cited two failed searches for hidden corpses; this one shows a clever way to search. The Gemara then identifies the pit as the one Ishmael son of Nethaniah filled with the dead in the book of Jeremiah.

people.name: Abba Shaul
people.about: The Sage who tells the story.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Hananya
people.about: An old man at Beit Horon who finds the hidden pit using wet sheets.

terms.meaning: An established belief that a place holds a corpse or part of one, which makes anyone who passes over it impure.

niddah-61a-16-16.note: A rumor spread that some men from the Galilee had killed someone. They came to Rabbi Tarfon and asked him to hide them. He said: what should I do? If I do not hide you, they will see you; but if I hide you, the Rabbis said that although one must not accept malicious talk as true, one must be wary of it. Go and hide yourselves.
niddah-61a-16-16.why: Rava has just taught that one must not believe malicious talk but must still be wary of it, drawn from Gedaliah, who ignored a warning and was killed. Rabbi Tarfon quotes that very rule.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: The Sage the men ask for shelter; he tells them to hide themselves.

terms.meaning: Harmful talk or rumor about another person, which the Torah forbids spreading or believing.

niddah-64b-18-18.note: A teaching of the Sages records an incident in which Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi gave a newly married virgin four nights, within the first twelve months of her marriage, during which blood after intercourse would be treated as blood of her torn hymen rather than menstrual blood. The text does not describe the case further.
niddah-64b-18-18.why: Rav has just ruled that a grown woman is given only the first night; the Gemara raises this incident as an objection and begins asking at what age the bride was.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who grants the bride the four nights.

terms.meaning: Bleeding from first intercourse, which does not make a woman ritually impure, unlike menstrual blood.
A status that, for a menstruating woman, forbids marital relations until she purifies herself.

niddah-65a-7-8.note: Minyamin Saksana was on his way to Shmuel's town, planning to rule as Rav had: to let a grown woman attribute bleeding to her hymen for the whole first night, even if she had already menstruated. He thought Rav made no distinction between a woman who had menstruated and one who had not. He died on the road before he arrived. Shmuel applied to Rav the verse 'No mishap shall befall the righteous.'
niddah-65a-7-8.why: Rav ruled that a grown woman gets the whole first night only if she has not yet menstruated. Minyamin was about to apply it without that condition, and his death is read as God keeping Rav's teaching from being misused.

people.name: Minyamin Saksana
people.about: A Sage who misread Rav's ruling and died on the way to apply it.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage to whose town Minyamin was going; he recites a verse about Rav.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Minyamin misunderstood.

terms.meaning: Here, a woman who has already had menstrual bleeding before her marriage.

niddah-66a-10-10.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi. He told Abdon to go and frighten her. Abdon did, and a mass of clotted blood fell from her. Rabbi said: this woman is cured.
niddah-66a-10-10.why: The baraita under discussion says that a woman who bleeds from intercourse on three occasions must be divorced. This case shows that such a woman can sometimes be cured.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whom the woman consults.

people.name: Abdon
people.about: A Sage whom Rabbi sends to frighten the woman.

niddah-66a-11-14.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Shmuel. He told Rav Dimi bar Yosef to go and frighten her, but when he did, nothing fell from her. Shmuel said she was filled with blood that falls out during intercourse, and that such a woman has no cure. Another woman told Rabbi Yohanan that every time she came up from the ritual bath she saw blood. He suggested the gossip of the women of her town had reached her, and told her to immerse in the river and be with her husband on its bank; others report he told her to tell her friends, so they would turn kind or pray for her. Rav Yosef said such a case happened in Pumbedita, and the woman was cured.
niddah-66a-11-14.why: The Gemara has just told how Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi had a bleeding woman frightened and a mass of blood fell from her, curing her. These cases follow as companions: the same remedy failing under Shmuel, and a different kind of bleeding treated by Rabbi Yohanan.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: A Sage to whom a woman who bled during intercourse came for help.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to frighten the woman.

people.name: Rabbi Yoḥanan
people.about: A Sage consulted by a woman who saw blood each time she left the ritual bath.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who reports a similar case in Pumbedita in which the woman was cured.

terms.meaning: A pool in which a woman immerses after her menstrual period ends; only after immersing may she resume relations with her husband.
A commandment; here, the required immersion that makes a woman permitted to her husband again.
A teaching of the early Sages not included in the Mishna, the core legal text the Gemara discusses.
A town in Babylonia, named here as the place of a similar case.

niddah-66a-22-22.note: Ravina arranged for his son to marry the daughter of Rav Hanina. Rav Hanina asked whether the marriage contract should set the wedding for Wednesday, and Ravina agreed. When Wednesday came, Ravina waited another week. Asked why, he cited Rava: a woman who accepts a marriage proposal must count seven clean days. Rav Hanina answered that Rava meant an adult woman who has seen blood, not a young girl who has not. Ravina replied that Rava had said so explicitly: the reason is that she desires her husband, and a young girl desires him too.
niddah-66a-22-22.why: The Gemara has just cited Rava's ruling that a woman who accepts a proposal must count seven clean days; this incident shows the ruling put into practice and extends it to a girl who has not yet menstruated.

people.name: Ravina
people.about: The father of the groom, who delays the wedding a week.

people.name: Rav Hanina
people.about: The father of the bride, who questions the delay.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage whose ruling Ravina follows.

terms.meaning: The ketuba, the document a groom gives his bride setting out his obligations, here also fixing the wedding date.
Seven days without any flow of blood, after which a woman immerses in a ritual bath and may resume marital relations.

niddah-66b-4-4.note: A maidservant of Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi immersed herself in a ritual bath. When she came up, a bone was found stuck between her teeth. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi required her to immerse again.
niddah-66b-4-4.why: The Gemara is discussing which parts of the body must be clean and free of anything blocking the water before immersion, even if the water need not reach them. The Gemara draws from this case that, for Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, nothing foreign may be even inside the mouth.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzḥak
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident, as quoted by Ravin bar Rav Adda.

people.name: Ravin bar Rav Adda
people.about: Passes on Rabbi Yitzhak's report of the incident.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose maidservant immersed; he ruled she must immerse again.

terms.meaning: Dipping the whole body in a ritual bath to become ritually pure; nothing may come between the body and the water.
Blocking: an object between the body and the water that can make an immersion invalid.

niddah-67b-17-17.note: Rav Adda recalled an incident to Rav Hinnana from Sura. The wife of Abba Mari, the Exilarch, quarreled with her husband and would not go to immerse so as to become permitted to him. Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak went to calm her, and she said: what can be done now? Come back tomorrow. He understood she meant she had not washed her hair in daylight, and answered: are you lacking kettles, buckets or servants?
niddah-67b-17-17.why: The Sages disagree whether a woman may wash her hair at night and immerse that same night; Rav Hinnana permits it. The Gemara reads Rav Nahman bar Yitzhak's reply as showing he too holds that washing and immersing the same night is permitted.

people.name: Rav Adda
people.about: Recalls this incident to Rav Hinnana from Sura.

people.name: Rav Ḥinnana from Sura
people.about: The Sage who permits washing the hair and immersing on the same night.

people.name: Abba Mari
people.about: The Exilarch, whose wife quarreled with him.

people.name: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak
people.about: Went to calm the Exilarch's wife and persuade her to immerse.

terms.meaning: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, a powerful official.
After her period a wife must immerse in a ritual bath, having first washed and combed her hair, before relations with her husband may resume.

niddah-69a-19-19.note: In the town of Galahi, the rule was that a man with one ox shepherded the town's herd for one day, and a man with no ox shepherded it for two. An orphan, the son of a widow, who had no oxen, was given the townspeople's oxen to shepherd, and he went and slaughtered them all. He told them that whoever had an ox should take one hide and whoever had none should take two. When they asked what he meant, he said the end of the law is like its beginning: if the man with no ox gets more at the start, he gets more at the end too.
niddah-69a-19-19.why: Rava has just mocked a ruling that a woman who saw no blood needs more immersions than one who did, calling it like the law of Galahi, where the man with no ox shepherds longer. The Gemara then tells this tale of Galahi.

people.name: orphan, the son of a widow
people.about: A boy with no oxen, given the town's oxen to shepherd, who slaughtered them.

terms.meaning: A place the Gemara says judged in the manner of Sodom, with unfair rules like this one.

niddah-66a-11-11.note: A woman who bled whenever she had intercourse came to Shmuel. He told Rav Dimi bar Yosef to go and frighten her. Rav Dimi did, but nothing fell from her. Shmuel said she was a woman who fills with blood and lets it out, and such a woman has no cure.
niddah-66a-11-11.why: Just before, Rabbi cured a woman the same way, when a mass of blood fell from her. Here the same method fails, showing it does not always work.

people.name: Shmuel
people.about: The Sage the woman consults; he sends Rav Dimi to frighten her.

people.name: Rav Dimi bar Yosef
people.about: Sent by Shmuel to frighten the woman.
